name: Botox nose tip lift

lead: A Botox nose tip lift relaxes the depressor septi nasi, a small muscle that tugs the nasal tip downward. Proponents say this lets a drooping tip sit a little higher, especially one that drops further when smiling or speaking.

Botulinum toxin blocks the signal from nerve to muscle, weakening the targeted muscle for a period of months, which reduces its downward pull on the tip. Effects are reported to last roughly two to four months, sometimes up to six. No clinical trials of the nasal tip use were located, so the size and duration of the effect are documented as practitioner claims.

paras: It is done in a clinic by an injector as a short-term alternative to surgery, and sometimes grouped with other non-surgical nose treatments. The effect fades as the toxin wears off, so users repeat it if they want to keep the look.

Botulinum toxin is prescription-only. Reported cosmetic adverse effects include weakness of nearby muscles, headache and allergic reactions, and the FDA has issued warnings about toxin spreading beyond the injection site. The nasal use is off-label, as cosmetic approvals concern glabellar (frown) lines.

angle.text: Proponents use botulinum toxin in the depressor septi nasi muscle as a short-term way to lift a drooping nasal tip, especially one that drops when smiling. Relaxing the muscle reduces its downward pull so the tip sits slightly higher. It is an off-label use with temporary results, and no published trials were located.

lead: A Botox nose tip lift is a cosmetic procedure in which botulinum toxin is injected into the depressor septi nasi muscle, a small muscle that pulls the nasal tip and the base of the nostrils downward, in order to relax it and allow the tip of the nose to sit slightly higher. It is sometimes grouped with other non-surgical nose treatments and is described by its proponents as a short-term alternative to surgery for a drooping tip, particularly one that drops further when a person smiles or speaks.[1]

The depressor septi nasi originates near the upper jaw and inserts into the nasal septum and the alar part of the nasalis muscle; it also moves the nasal tip when the upper lip moves.[1] Botulinum toxin products are prescription-only in the United States, UK and EU, and their effects are reported to last roughly two to four months, sometimes up to six.[2]

The nasal tip use is an off-label application: regulatory approvals for cosmetic botulinum toxin concern glabellar (frown) lines, and the sources reviewed for this entry describe no approved labelling for the nose.[2] No clinical trials of nasal tip injection were located for this article, so the effect size and duration of the procedure are documented here only as practitioner claims.
infobox: Months; botulinum toxin effects generally 2-4 months[2]
Botulinum toxin is prescription-only (US, UK, EU)[2]

paras: The procedure targets the depressor septi nasi, which pulls the nasal tip and columella downward, narrowing the nostrils; it acts as an antagonist to other nasal muscles.[1] Practitioners say that relaxing the muscle reduces downward pull on the tip, which can make a tip that dips on smiling appear less drooped. The Wikipedia entry on the muscle notes only that surgeons reposition its head during rhinoplasty to help ensure normal nose position afterward, and does not discuss toxin treatment.[1]

Cosmetic use of botulinum toxin was first described in 1989 and the FDA approved Botox Cosmetic for glabellar lines in 2002.[2] Smoothing generally appears within several days and peaks around one week.[2] Reported adverse effects in cosmetic use include unintended muscle weakness or paralysis of nearby muscles, headache, flu-like symptoms and allergic reactions; the FDA issued warnings in 2008 and added boxed warnings in 2009 concerning spread of toxin beyond the injection site.[2]

The procedure appears in lists of non-surgical nose treatments as a way to lift a drooping tip without surgery. Descriptions in appearance communities generally present it as a temporary adjustment that wears off as the toxin effect fades; no community sources were reviewed for this entry.

timeline.event: Aesthetic use of botulinum toxin first described.[2]
FDA approves Botox Cosmetic for glabellar lines.[2]
Boxed warnings added to botulinum toxin products in the US.[2]
